title: A Cellar for the Hymn
premise: Mirabel Thackeray takes a teaching post in the remote village of Hollowmere, where students vanish one by one and every record of them is quietly erased. Beneath the schoolhouse cellar she finds a door sealed from the inside and learns the founders' hymn is not worship but a binding: something beneath the school must be fed, or it will walk free. As the village closes ranks around the ritual, Mirabel must choose between exposing the truth and completing the hymn herself, because the last voice required is a teacher's, and the previous one never left the cellar. In the end she sings the final verse with the missing children's names woven in, sealing the door with justice instead of silence, and stays in Hollowmere as its keeper.
about_author: Orsen Ashgrove is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent nine years in one-room schoolhouses across the northern counties before turning to writing. They collect hymnals, and their fiction draws on the folk rituals and quiet cruelties of small communities that protect themselves at any cost.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Things
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. She arrives in Hollowmere, takes the schoolhouse post, and begins her habit of documenting everything in her ledger. The village feels watchful but welcoming, and the emotional beat is cautious hope: a woman who has never belonged anywhere deciding to try again.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Her first week of classes goes well until she counts heads and comes up one short. The register says eleven students; she has counted ten all day. The headmistress, Mrs. Corvel, corrects the ledger without explanation. The beat is the first cold prickle of wrongness.

chapters.title: The Chalk Circle
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. She finds chalked names under the floorboards of the cloakroom, dozens of them, each crossed out. A student, Wren, whispers that the crossed-out children 'went down for singing practice.' Mirabel documents it. The beat is dread disguised as curiosity.

chapters.title: Excavation
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. The council hires a crew to shore up the schoolhouse foundations after a winter flood. Mirabel watches from her window as the first shovels bite into the cellar floor. The beat is complicity: she says nothing, and hates herself for it.

chapters.title: A Door Sealed From the Inside
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. The crew unearths an iron door with no handle on their side, its bolts thrown from within. The foreman refuses to touch it further and leaves that night without pay. Mrs. Corvel thanks Mirabel for her discretion. The beat is vertigo.

chapters.title: The Founders' Hymn
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. In the village archive she finds the founders' hymnal, its final page a verse marked 'For the Keeper, sung alone.' Marginal notes list dates, and each date matches a vanished child. The beat is horror arriving as scholarship.

chapters.title: Wren's Question
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Wren asks her directly whether she will be the next keeper, and whether that is why teachers never stay. Mirabel lies badly. That night she hears faint humming through the cellar floor. The beat is guilt and the first pull of obligation.

chapters.title: The Village That Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. She confronts the innkeeper, the sexton, and finally old Tam Hallow, who tells her the truth: the thing below was the founders' punishment for a crime the law would not touch, and it must be fed names and song or it takes them itself. The beat is terrible understanding.

chapters.title: What the Law Would Not Touch
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel, with Tam's long flashback. The founders' hymn was born from an unpunished atrocity: a magistrate who destroyed a family and walked free. The cellar door is a courtroom. The beat is moral inversion—Mirabel realizes the horror has a kind of justice in it.

chapters.title: The Erased Register
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. She compares her ledger to the school records and proves the vanished children were real, scrubbed from every document but her own handwriting. Mrs. Corvel discovers her snooping and, gently, asks her to leave. The beat is isolation.

chapters.title: Staying
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. She burns her return ticket and tells Corvel she will finish what the founders started—on her terms. Corvel, relieved and ashamed, gives her the keeper's key. The beat is resolve hardening into commitment.

chapters.title: First Lesson Below
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. She unlocks the door and descends, ledger in hand, into a cellar that is larger inside than out, lined with desks facing a dark that listens. She reads the children's names aloud and the dark hums them back. The beat is awe braided with terror.

chapters.title: The Voice in the Dark
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Something in the cellar speaks with the voice of the previous teacher, who never left. It explains the ritual's mechanics and its hunger, and warns that the binding is weakening because the village stopped believing in its own sin. The beat is a bargain taking shape.

chapters.title: Hymn Practice
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. She teaches the surviving children the founders' hymn as ordinary music, hiding the ritual inside a lesson. Wren suspects and helps anyway, asking only that the vanished children's names be sung. The beat is found family forming in the dark.

chapters.title: The Council Objects
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. The village council, fearing exposure more than the thing below, moves to seal the schoolhouse with everyone inside and let the ritual fail on its own terms. Tam Hallow is silenced. The beat is betrayal by the community she came to join.

chapters.title: What It Takes When It's Starving
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. The binding frays: cold spreads through the school, the crossed-out names begin reappearing on walls, and a child nearly walks into the cellar in her sleep. Mirabel realizes the ritual cannot wait for the solstice. The beat is the clock starting to run.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. She writes her own history in the ledger—every place she was invisible, every wrong she let pass—and understands the hymn requires a voice that has chosen to be seen. The beat is the theme crystallizing: belonging must be claimed, not hidden into.

chapters.title: Breaking the Seal
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel and Wren alternating. They open the schoolhouse to the whole village, forcing every adult to stand at the cellar door and hear what their silence has fed. Some flee; some stay. The beat is the community forced to witness.

chapters.title: The Final Verse
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. In the cellar's dark classroom she sings the founders' verse alone, but rewrites it as she goes, naming the vanished children and the magistrate's crime aloud, making the thing below a witness rather than a wound. The beat is the climax: terror transfigured into ceremony.

chapters.title: Sealed From the Inside, Again
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. The door closes itself, the bolts turning from within, and the humming stops—but the previous teacher's voice remains, faintly, asking to be remembered. Mirabel writes her name in the ledger's margin. The beat is exhausted, grieving relief.

chapters.title: The New Register
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel. Spring comes. She restores the erased children to the school register, teaches their story openly, and the village, changed, lets her. Corvel resigns; Tam Hallow helps rebuild. The beat is justice outside the law becoming justice inside the community.

chapters.title: A Cellar for the Hymn
chapters.summary: POV Mirabel, years later. A new teacher arrives, nervous and invisible-feeling, and Mirabel hands over the ledger and the key, explaining that the door is sealed but listening, and that the hymn must never again be sung in secret. The beat is continuity: belonging passed on, the horror tended rather than hidden.
